lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Make two groups for: foil, tissue, rubber glove, ceramic mug using “flexible vs rigid”. Where does each go?

FEEDBACK
Foil and glove flexible; mug rigid; tissue flexible (tears) — accept reasoned placements.

WATCH FOR
Sorting by colour when the question asks for strength mixes property types.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Create three different property sorts for the same twelve materials. Write the rule above each sort. Photograph or sketch one finished sort.

Write a short reflection naming one observation or step you corrected and why.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Rule: floats or sinks in water. Cork floats; coin sinks. Another rule: transparent / opaque. Clear cup vs wooden block.

Make two groups for: foil, tissue, rubber glove, ceramic mug using “flexible vs rigid”. Where does each go?

FEEDBACK
Foil and glove flexible; mug rigid; tissue flexible (tears) — accept reasoned placements.
teach_steps.explain:
Sorting materials by properties uses a clear rule (for example waterproof vs absorbent) so every item has a place.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the observations, properties or test steps that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a result is uncertain, identify what would have to be observed or tested again. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
